title: Phase transition and bandgap modulation in TiO<sub>2</sub> nanostructures for enhanced visible-light activity and environmental applications.

sections.heading: Experimental method
sections.text: Experimental method We purchased Aluminum (III) chloride hexahydrate (AlCl 3 .6H 12 O 6 , Purity 99.999%), titanium (III) chloride hexahydrate (TiCl 3 . 6H 2 O, Purity 99.999%), thiourea (SC(NH 2 ) 2 , 99.9%) and sodium hydroxide (NaOH, Purity 99.999%) from Alfa-Aser. Through the experiment, Alfa aser-made de-ionized water was used to synthesize the samples. First, 2 g of TiCl 3 .6H 2 O was added in one beker containing 50 ml (ml) of deionized water and starred for 30 min. Second, 0.5 g of NaOH was added to the second beaker with 20 ml of deionized water for 20 min. Then aforementioned NaOH liquid medium was conventionally added dropwise through a pipet to 50 ml of TiCl 3 . 6H 2 O solution and allowed to stand at room temperature for 10 min before being magnetically stirred. The mentioned solution was vigorously stirred for 50 min to ensure a homogenous solution. Finally, the stirred solvent was transferred to a 100 ml stainless steel Teflon line autoclave and kept for reaction under 150 °C for 24 h. The temperature of the solution in the oven was gradually raised to 150 °C. Following centrifugation, the resultant solution was repeatedly washed several times with deionized water until it reached a pH of 7. The resulting mixture was transferred into a beaker and allowed to dry for 24 h at 60 °C in an oven. Furhtermore, Aluminum nitrate nonahydrate (Al(NO₃)₃·9H 2 O) and sodium sulfate (Na 2 SO₄) were employed as sources of Al 3 ⁺/Al 2 ⁺ and S⁶⁺, respectively with the mixture of TiCl 3 .6H 2 O in one beaker containing 50 ml (ml) of deionized water and stirred for 30 min. The molar ratio of dopants to Ti was maintained at 2%. To facilitate uniform precipitation, the pH of the solution was adjusted to ~ 9 using ammonium hydroxide. The gel was dried at 100 °C for 12 h, then calcined at 500 °C for 3 h in air to achieve crystallinity and dopant inclusion. The progressive temperature increase (5 °C/min) resulted in regulated phase development. Finally, the pure TiO 2  (named = P) nanoparticles were at the bottom of the beaker. The same process was used to 2%-Al and 2% (named = X1), 4% (named = X2), 6% (named = X3), and 8% (named = X4) S co-doped TiO 2 , only the difference is the first beaker was contain TiCl 3 . 6H 2 O + AlCl 3 .6H 12 O 6+ SC(NH 2 ) 2 . The schematic diagram of Fig.  1  shows the detailed hydrothermal routes. Fig. 1 The process flow diagram for the synthesis of titanium dioxide nanoparticles. The GSAS suite of the Rietveld assessment tool was performed on a PAN analytical-made X-ray diffraction (XRD) diffractometer (Model EMPYREAN) using Cu Kα (λ = 1.54059 Å) radiations data. The structure was characterized using XRD results. The lattice parameters and volumes were obtained utilizing typical Rietveld refinements via software (High Score Plus). UV–vis spectrophotometer (UV cuvette with a path length of 10 mm) was used to measure the bandgap of the materials and photocatalytic degradation. The nanoparticles and their elemental analysis were analyzed using Joel-made energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) spectroscopy (Joel 7600F, Tokyo, Japan) at 10 kV combined with the scanning electron microscope (SEM). The particle size and their related lattice plans and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern were measured through Joel-made (JEM-120i -Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM). To estimate the lattice characteristics, such as the spacing between atoms (d-spacing), size (volume), and Rietveld refinements were performed using new High Score Plus software. Bruker-made Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) was used to measure phase composition. Microwave absorption spectroscopy was measured by using Keysight made 1 GHz to 18 GHz using HP8722ES network analyzer. The P and X series photoluminescence (PL) spectra were acquired using a 355 nm pulsed laser with an excitation of 235 Hz along with. a cut-off filter at 370 nm.
